title: Visual Space Perception and Visually Directed Action
research_question: This work investigates whether natural environments viewed binocularly from a stationary vantage point are perceived correctly, and how the properties of visually perceived space relate to visually directed action, particularly open-loop motoric tasks. The central aim is to reconcile seemingly contradictory results from psychophysical matching tasks (showing distortions) and visually directed action tasks (showing accuracy).

participants.description: Experiment 1 & 2: 10 men (20-33 years old for Exp 1, 18-33 years old for Exp 2), students at the University of São Paulo, Brazil, with at least 20/20 visual acuity (corrected or uncorrected), active nonprofessional players of soccer, volleyball, or basketball. Experiment 3: 5 graduate students (24-29 years old) at the University of California, Santa Barbara, with 20/20 visual acuity.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Experiments 1 & 2: A large grassy field (35m x 20m) with a grid of white lines (1m squares) and a central axis. Targets were white steel rods (16cm high, 1cm diameter) sharpened at one end. Experiment 1 used frontal intervals (1.0, 1.5, 2.0m) at 4, 6, 8, 10, or 12m from the origin, and subjects adjusted depth intervals. Experiment 2 used a first target directly in front (4, 6, 8, 10, or 12m) and a second target (1.0, 1.5, 2.0m away) either in depth or width. Experiment 3: A lightproof warehouse (35m x 20m) with a square workspace (1200cm side). A single red neon lamp target placed on the ground at the center. Parallel straight paths (6m long) marked on the ground, with nearest approach distances of 100, 200, or 400 cm to the target.

measures.construct: Perceived exocentric interval length (depth vs. frontal)
measures.instrument: Psychophysical matching task (subjective adjustment of depth interval to match frontal interval)
Blind walking to previously viewed target(s)
Continuous blind pointing with the right arm while walking

findings.antecedent: Physical depth intervals on the ground plane (compared to frontal intervals)
findings.mechanism: Perceptual foreshortening of depth intervals, requiring them to be physically larger to appear equal to frontal intervals.
findings.quote: the depth intervals had to be made much larger in order to be judged equal to the width intervals

findings.consequent: Physical inequality required for equal perceived length (depth vs. frontal)
findings.mechanism: Perceptual foreshortening of depth intervals increases with egocentric distance.
findings.quote: this physical inequality of equal-appearing intervals increasing with egocentric distance

findings.mechanism: Visually directed walking is accurate and linear, suggesting accurate egocentric distance perception for action.
findings.quote: virtually perfect linearity of the walking response

findings.consequent: Mean signed error in blind walking to the first target
findings.mechanism: Small, non-systematic undershoot in blind walking to a single target.
findings.quote: The mean signed error for all subjects and targets was 55 cm, indicating an undershoot on average

findings.antecedent: Previously viewed second target location relative to the first
findings.consequent: Mean signed angular error in blind walking to the second target
findings.mechanism: Accurate spatial updating for target direction during blind locomotion.
findings.quote: The mean signed angular error was 0.27 deg

findings.antecedent: Physical depth intervals on the ground plane (compared to frontal intervals)
findings.mechanism: Perceptual foreshortening of depth intervals, consistent with Experiment 1.
findings.quote: The results are very much like those in Figure 3a

findings.consequent: Physical inequality required for equal perceived length (depth vs. frontal)
findings.mechanism: Perceptual foreshortening increases with egocentric distance, more apparent than in Experiment 1.
findings.quote: the increase in ratio with egocentric distance was more apparent for all three intervals

findings.consequent: Mean signed error in blind walking to the first target
findings.mechanism: Small, non-systematic undershoot in blind walking to a single target, similar to Experiment 1.
findings.quote: mean signed error was -27 cm (undershoot) and the mean absolute error was 57 cm

findings.consequent: Blind walked distance to the first target
findings.mechanism: Near-linearity of walking response, indicating accurate egocentric distance perception for action.
findings.quote: power function exponents were .98 and .96, indicating near-linearity of the responses.

findings.antecedent: Previously viewed interval between two targets (frontal or sagittal)
findings.mechanism: Systematic overestimation of intervals in blind walking.
findings.quote: the mean intervals were on the average about 50 cm larger than the corresponding physical intervals

findings.antecedent: Previously viewed frontal vs. sagittal intervals
findings.consequent: Ratio of walked width response interval to depth response interval
findings.mechanism: Visually directed walking does not manifest the perceptual anisotropy (foreshortening of depth intervals) observed in matching tasks.
findings.quote: walking to two targets does not manifest this anisotropy

findings.consequent: Continuous blind pointing direction while walking
findings.mechanism: Accurate imaginal updating of target location during self-motion, supporting correct egocentric distance perception.
findings.quote: the mean pointing direction nearly coincides with that of the target for all three paths

findings.antecedent: Walking path (100cm nearest approach to target)
findings.consequent: Angular velocity of the arm during continuous blind pointing
findings.mechanism: Angular velocity changes systematically in accord with the true target azimuth, indicating real-time spatial updating rather than preprogrammed movement.
findings.quote: the angular velocity of the arm... changes systematically during the trav- erse in accord with the true target azimuth.

mechanisms: Perceptual foreshortening of depth intervals (leading to non-veridical perception in matching tasks)
Accurate egocentric distance perception (Hypothesis 1, supported by walking/pointing tasks)
Cognitive correction of misperceived distance (Hypothesis 2, unconscious learning allows mapping between distorted perception and accurate action)
Separation of visual systems (Hypothesis 3, one for conscious perception, one for visuomotor coordination)
Imaginal updating of target location during self-motion
Independence of perceived exocentric distance from perceived egocentric distance (proposed to reconcile matching and walking results)
moderators: Task type (perceptual matching vs. visually directed action)
limitations: The interval matching task required subjects to respond to exocentric intervals, while the walking task involved responding to absolute positions, making direct comparison challenging (Experiment 1).
Blind walking to two targets might not be a strictly exocentric response, as subjects could guide locomotion to each absolute position successively (Experiment 2).
The matching and walking tasks may not be strictly comparable due to different response types (perceptual comparison vs. responding to absolute locations).
The first target in walking tasks was always directly in front of the origin of locomotion, limiting the range of target positions.
Potential for reduced cue availability in the darkened room for Experiment 3, though not explicitly stated as a limitation for this study, it's discussed in relation to other studies.
